newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bombing raises concern over security in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Bombing raises concern over security in Bosnia.

text.p: Western envoys said on Monday that a bomb blast outside international offices in Bosnia's Serb-controlled territory did not represent an organised retaliatory campaign for a NATO raid on suspected war criminals.

Two kg (four pounds) of plastic explosives destroyed an OSCE pickup truck in the eastern town of Zvornik on Sunday evening and shattered windows nearby but caused no casualties, officials from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe said.

The bombing outside OSCE and United Nations offices was the only serious violence reported since British soldiers seized one suspected war criminal and shot dead another who resisted arrest last week, NATO said.
"We are following the situation carefully but the situation on the ground remains calm," alliance spokesman Major Chris Riley told Reuters.

In the past, NATO commanders had been reluctant to go after indicted war criminals partly because they feared such operations would trigger attacks on peacekeeping troops and disrupt relations with rival armies.
The United Nations, the OSCE and other envoys played down a possible security threat and said they had no plans to evacuate staff members from Serb territory.

A spokesman for the High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, said the bombing would not undermine international resolve to see suspects extradited to the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
"Life goes on as normal," Duncan Bullivant told reporters. "We do not see a widespread, orchestrated security problem. We see isolated incidents."

Bosnian Serb nationalist leaders have sharply criticised last Thursday's action, and on Monday expressed anger over the sentencing on Monday of Dusan Tadic, a Serb convicted of atrocities by the U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia. Tadic was sentenced to 20 years.

But the Serb leaders have refrained from inciting the population to take up arms in revenge and have struck a much more cautious tone than in wartime, when they defied Western governments with shelling attacks on Sarajevo and abductions of U.N. peacekeeping soldiers.
The Bosnian Serb military, once the dominant military force in Bosnia, is now strictly supervised by the alliance-led force and its heavy weapons have been placed in storage sites.
Diplomats said it was no coincidence that the bombing attack occurred outside the offices of unarmed monitors instead of the bases manned by heavily armed NATO troops.
"It's an easy target," said one Western diplomat.
Serb authorities in their headquarters in Pale, outside Sarajevo, threatened to stop attending meetings in the Bosnian capital because they said they felt unsafe after the NATO raid.

Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's multi-ethnic collective presidency, did not show up for a scheduled presidency session in predominantly Moslem Sarajevo on Friday, a day after the NATO operation.
Bullivant said the move amounted to "political gameplaying" and dismissed Serb complaints about the tribunal's use of sealed indictments.
"If they've done something for which they should be indicted, then quite rightly they should feel nervous," he said.
Bullivant said Serb television coverage of the NATO operation was full of "disinformation and outrageous comments" and would not be tolerated indefinitely.

Diplomats said major powers were considering jamming the Serb television signal if necessary and broadcasting Radio Free Europe or the Voice of America to Bosnia in a bid to counter reports coming out of Karadzic's media.
